clue.text: Right to hop a small distance in imperishable body part

indicators.text: to hop a small distance in
indicators.note: a letter that hops a short way along a word drops back in at a new spot, so 'right' lands a couple of places earlier inside 'imperishable'

blocks.note: imperishable = never-ending, lasting for ever
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone claims the right to hop a short way inside some everlasting part of the body.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the R out of NEVER-ENDING and hop it two places towards the front: NEVER becomes NERVE, and the whole thing becomes NERVE ENDING.
explanation.definitionFit: A nerve ending is the tip of a nerve fibre in skin or tissue, so it is literally a small anatomical piece of you.

clue.text: Country pub abandoned, amphibian jumping about

indicators.note: whatever is abandoned is left behind, so the word for 'pub' is dropped from the creature
a frog jumping about ends up anywhere, so the remaining letters of the creature land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
PH, for public house, is the map abbreviation for a pub

explanation.surface: A country pub has been left empty, with a frog or toad hopping around the deserted bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove P and H from AMPHIBIAN to leave AMIBIAN, then rearrange those seven letters. 'Country pub' wants to be one phrase; 'Country' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Namibia is a nation in south-west Africa, bordering Angola and South Africa, so it is simply an example of a country.

clue.text: Once more considers the dilapidated skating venues seen around

indicators.note: something dilapidated has fallen apart, so the letters of 'the' come apart and reassemble
the ice venues are seen around the scrambled word, so they wrap it

blocks.note: skating venues are ice rinks
the three letters of 'the', rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone reconsiders plans after seeing the run-down state of local ice rinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The scrambled 'the' goes after the R of RINKS: R-ETH-INKS.
explanation.definitionFit: To rethink is to think again about a decision, so the verb means reconsidering it a second time.

clue.text: Nobleman in Cockney cast

indicators.note: a Londoner's accent drops the opening H, so the word for 'cast' is to be heard as a Cockney says it

blocks.note: cast = hurl, which a Cockney says without its H

explanation.surface: A lord turns up among the cast of an East End play.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class East London accent, famous for dropping H: 'hurl' becomes 'url, which sounds like the title.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is a British peer ranking above a viscount and below a marquess, a titled member of the aristocracy.

clue.text: In atrium: nuts, bananas, flower with edible leaves

indicators.note: to go bananas is to go crazy, so the letters of the words before it go wild

blocks.note: the fodder, ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A list of things found in a conservatory: nuts, bananas and a salad flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' and 'bananas' both look like anagram indicators sitting in a list of produce; 'nuts' is fodder and 'bananas' does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Nasturtiums are bright garden plants whose peppery leaves and blooms are commonly eaten in salads.

clue.text: The writer thinks highly of being furious

blocks.note: the writer refers to themself as I
to rate someone is to think highly of them

explanation.surface: An author admires somebody for being angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the setter speaking of themself, which gives I; then comes RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Irate is a direct synonym for very angry, the adjectival state of someone losing their temper.

clue.text: Gigantic old leviathan; in allegory, tempting hubris, primarily?

definitions.text: Gigantic old leviathan; in allegory, tempting hubris, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so each of the preceding words gives only its opening letter

blocks.clueFragment: Gigantic old leviathan; in allegory, tempting hubris
blocks.note: the first letters of seven words in a row

explanation.surface: A description of a biblical giant as a symbol of pride tempting fate.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the initials spell the giant, and the words describe him, the huge figure of the Bible story whose arrogance brought him down.
explanation.definitionFit: Goliath was the huge Philistine warrior felled by young David, a stock example of pride before a fall.

clue.text: Following drink, goes off with summer clothing

indicators.note: the second part follows the first, so 'goes off with' comes after the word for 'drink'

blocks.note: a short is a small measure of spirits
to trouser money is to pocket it and make off with it

explanation.surface: Someone has a drink and then heads out wearing their summer outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes off with' reads as leaving, but in British slang to trouser something is to pocket it, often dishonestly. A short is a spirit such as whisky, as opposed to a long drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Shorts, or short trousers, are knee-length legwear worn when the weather is hot.

clue.text: Love to tuck into desserts such as honey bun and treacle

definitions.text: such as honey bun and treacle

indicators.note: to tuck into puddings is to go inside them, so the word for 'love' goes inside the word for 'desserts'

blocks.note: sweets = desserts, puddings
love is nil, nothing, in a tennis score

explanation.surface: Someone loves eating desserts, such as a honey bun and treacle tart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Honey bun' and 'treacle' look like more desserts; they are pet names whispered to a lover. SWEETS is the British word for dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet nothings are the affectionate endearments lovers murmur, and honey bun and treacle are examples of those pet names.

clue.text: Rodent spotted in Birmingham's terrarium

indicators.note: something spotted in a place is visible inside it, so the answer sits within the next words

blocks.note: it runs from the end of the city across the apostrophe into the glass tank

explanation.surface: A small animal has been seen in a glass tank belonging to a Birmingham household.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the apostrophe, which the solver simply ignores.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamster is a small burrowing pet with cheek pouches, a member of the rodent family alongside mice and rats.

clue.text: Accept a fork-tailed songbird

blocks.note: a verb for believing a story without question, as in taking it down whole
the migrant bird with a deeply forked tail

explanation.walkthrough: Two meanings of one word side by side: a verb for believing something and a summer migrant bird.
explanation.definitionFit: To swallow a claim is idiomatically to believe it; the bird is the familiar summer visitor with streamers on its tail.

clue.text: Religious leader's nearly bang on

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the phrase meaning 'bang on' loses its final letter

blocks.note: to bang on and to rabbit on both mean to talk at tedious length; the last letter goes

explanation.surface: A religious leader's sermon is nearly spot on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bang on' reads as exactly right, but in British speech it also means to talk on and on, as does 'rabbit on'. Drop the T from RABBIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is a Jewish scholar and teacher who leads a synagogue congregation.

clue.text: Aren't emus, largely, surprisingly, able to do sums?

indicators.note: largely means for the most part, so the birds' name keeps most of its letters but not its last
the letters turn up in a surprising order, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored
EMUS without its last letter

explanation.surface: A mock-serious question about whether big flightless birds are, unexpectedly, good at arithmetic.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in the first word is ignored, and only three letters of the birds are used.
explanation.definitionFit: Numerate is the maths counterpart of literate, describing someone competent with numbers and arithmetic.

clue.text: No end in turmoil brewing by car showroom?

indicators.note: no end means the chaos word loses its last letter
something brewing is stirred and in ferment, so the remaining letters are mixed

blocks.note: Audi is a German car make
TURMOIL with its end removed

explanation.surface: Chaos is brewing endlessly at a car dealership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Car showroom' looks like one phrase, but the car is AUDI and 'showroom?' is the definition, a room where shows are staged; the question mark flags that pun.
explanation.definitionFit: An auditorium is the hall of a theatre where audiences watch performances, so punningly a room for shows.

clue.text: Pursue legal cases in casual apparel

blocks.note: to track someone is to pursue them
lawsuits are legal cases

explanation.surface: A lawyer fights court battles while dressed down in leisurewear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suits' looks like the formal wear a lawyer would choose; here it means lawsuits.
explanation.definitionFit: Tracksuits are loose sporty jacket-and-trouser sets worn for comfort and leisure, informal clothing.

clue.text: At which time, novel about hotel gets rejected

indicators.note: about means around, so the novel word goes around the letter for 'hotel'
something rejected is sent back, so the whole assembly is turned back to front

blocks.note: novel = new, fresh
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A novel set around a hotel has been turned down by a publisher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' wants to be a book, but it is the adjective: NE(H)W, then reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: When as a conjunction or adverb asks or states the moment something happens, the time at which it occurs.

clue.text: Piano, perhaps it includes D# and F# (according to Spooner)

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the phrase for the notes has its initial sounds exchanged

blocks.note: the B major chord is B, D sharp and F sharp; swap the opening sounds of 'B chord'

explanation.surface: A musician points out that a particular instrument has certain sharps on it.
explanation.walkthrough: D sharp and F sharp are the black notes of the B major triad, so 'it' is a B chord; swapping the B and K sounds gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A piano is the classic instrument played with a row of keys, and electronic ones are called by the same name.

clue.text: Get rid of unevenly shaved moustache

indicators.note: shaving trims from both sides, and unevenly means one letter comes off the front but four off the back

blocks.note: the M is shaved from the front and ACHE from the back

explanation.surface: Someone wants to be rid of a badly trimmed moustache.
explanation.walkthrough: Unlike an even trim, which would take the same number of letters from each end, this one takes one from the front and four from the back.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust someone is to force them out of a position, to remove or expel them.

clue.text: Suspends items of furniture

blocks.note: to put a plan on hold, as in postponing a project indefinitely
flat boards fixed to a wall or in a bookcase

explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspends' suggests hanging things up, which shelves also do, but here it is the verb for postponing.
explanation.definitionFit: A project that is shelved is put aside indefinitely; as a plural noun the word names storage boards in bookcases.

clue.text: Sees bodily shape getting portly, shedding first of two tons

indicators.note: shedding means casting off, so the word for 'portly' loses the first of its two T letters

blocks.note: one's figure is one's bodily shape

blocks.clueFragment: portly, shedding first of two tons
blocks.note: STOUT = portly; it has two Ts (T for ton), and the first goes

explanation.surface: Someone notices their figure getting fat and wants to lose a couple of tons.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'two tons' are the two Ts in STOUT, T being the abbreviation for ton; only the first is shed.
explanation.definitionFit: To see a solution is to understand or work it out, and figures out is the phrasal verb for that.

clue.text: 'On Her Majesty's Service' on fronts of letters aligned with current regulation?

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter, so the three words that follow each give only their opening

blocks.note: OHMS is the abbreviation printed on British government post
the initials of the three words

explanation.surface: Official government envelopes are checked to see that they comply with the latest rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current regulation' reads as today's rules; the question mark says current means electric. OHMS was stamped on official British mail.
explanation.definitionFit: Ohm's law states that electric flow through a conductor is proportional to voltage, a rule governing electricity.

clue.text: Farm animal breaking speed of light ... take off ... lift off!

indicators.note: to take off is to remove, so the letters of the word 'lift' come out of the physics phrase
the phrase is broken up, so its remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the phrase taken as written
these four letters are the ones removed

explanation.surface: A rocket-launch countdown in which some farm animal breaks the light barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: The launch imagery hides the instruction: remove L, I, F and T from SPEEDOFLIGHT, leaving eight letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheepdog is a working dog such as a collie trained to herd flocks, kept on farms.

clue.text: Dance round trailer?

blocks.note: a prom is a formal school dance
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A dance performed around a trailer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like a container instruction around PROM, but it is simply the letter O added.
explanation.definitionFit: A film trailer is a short promotional clip, and promo is the informal term for such an advertisement.

clue.text: All but last two of Italian children seeing cartoon

indicators.note: all but the last two means everything except the final pair, so the Italian word is cut short

blocks.note: BAMBINI is Italian for children; its final NI goes

explanation.surface: Italian kids are watching an animated film.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the Disney fawn's name comes from the same root, the Italian word for a baby.
explanation.definitionFit: Bambi is the 1942 Disney animated film about a young deer, a famous animation.

clue.text: Everyman's behind essentially nasty fizz

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so only the middle of the adjective is kept
the setter's letter is behind, following the kept middle

blocks.note: the inside three letters, without the N and Y
Everyman is the setter, who refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: The setter owns up to being behind some unpleasant bubbly.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the name of this puzzle's setter, so it stands for I; 'Everyman's behind' means I comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a sparkling Italian white wine from Piedmont, and fizz is informal for any bubbly wine.

clue.text: Rector and associate fiddle endlessly with pasta dish

indicators.note: endlessly means without an end, so the instrument word loses its final letter

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for rector
A is the abbreviation for associate, as in qualifications such as ARCM
a fiddle is a violin, cut short

explanation.surface: A vicar and a colleague keep playing about with their dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' looks like fidgeting with food, but it is the violin.
explanation.definitionFit: Ravioli are small square pasta parcels filled with meat or cheese, a classic Italian meal.

clue.text: Only half seasoned, bear with difficulty a gastropod

indicators.note: only half of the word survives, so the back four letters of 'seasoned' are dropped

blocks.note: the first four of its eight letters
to lug is to carry something heavy with effort

explanation.surface: Someone struggles to carry a snail that is only half cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seasoned' suggests cooking, but only its first half, SEAS, is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea slugs are shell-less marine molluscs, and molluscs of that class are gastropods, like snails.

clue.text: Charge one that may have a tab for extra glass

blocks.note: to storm is to charge at, attack

blocks.clueFragment: one that may have a tab
blocks.note: a browser window can hold several tabs

explanation.surface: Someone is charged for the additional glass of wine that went on their bar tab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tab' and 'glass' suggest a bar bill, but the tab is in a web browser, and the glass is glazing.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm window is a second pane fitted outside an ordinary window for insulation, additional glazing.
